---
title: "Make a model for your cells"
---

OMERO-Screen segments nuclei and cells with
[Cellpose](https://www.cellpose.org). Without further setup it uses a default
that suits the machine:

| Machine | Default |
|---|---|
| NVIDIA GPU (Linux workstation, HPC) | Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`), good on most images |
| Mac or CPU | the stock Cellpose 3 models: `nuclei` for nuclei, `cyto3` for cells |

The stock Cellpose 3 models segment most fixed cells reasonably. On a 10x DAPI
plate they found 616 nuclei where a custom lab model found 606 and Cellpose 4
found 621. They do worse on unusual stains, very dense or very sparse cells,
other magnifications and live-cell DNA dyes. A model trained on a few of
**your** images, with **your** microscope, usually fixes that.

Every processed plate records which models were used (map annotation
`omero-screen/provenance` on the plate), so you can always check.

## Train a model with the Cellpose GUI

Training is done in the Cellpose desktop app, with you correcting its masks
("human in the loop"). Install it once:

```bash
uv tool install --python 3.12 "cellpose[gui]<4"
```

1. **Export a few representative images**, say 5–10 fields covering your
   conditions, for example from napari (*File → Save Selected Layer*) as TIFF.
   Use the channel you segment on (DAPI/Hoechst for nuclei).
2. **Open them**: run `cellpose`, then drag in the first image.
3. **Start from the closest model.** Choose `nuclei` (or `cyto3`) under
   *Model zoo*, run it, then correct the masks: delete wrong ones (Ctrl+click on
   the mask), draw missing ones (right-click, then trace the outline).
4. **Train**: *Models → Train new model*, start from the same model, keep the
   defaults. Cellpose saves the new model in a `models` folder next to your
   images; copy the model file into `~/.cellpose/models/` when you are done.
5. **Repeat on the next image** with your new model; each round needs fewer
   corrections. Three or four images are often enough.

The [Cellpose documentation](https://cellpose.readthedocs.io/en/v3.1.1.1/gui.html)
covers the GUI in detail.

## Use it in OMERO-Screen

Name your model in the user config (`~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`), per
role or cell line:

```toml
[segmentation.models]
nuclei = "my_nuclei_model"     # file name in ~/.cellpose/models
RPE = "my_rpe_cells_model"     # cell segmentation for cell lines containing "RPE"
```

Cell lines are matched by name (exact, then contained in the plate's cell
line), so `RPE` covers "RPE-1 WT". A cell line without an entry uses the `U2OS`
entry, or the device default if none is configured. For a single run you can
also override everything: `omero-screen 1234 --model cp3:my_model`.

## Share models in a lab

Models a whole lab uses can go into the lab's site profile as a **model set**,
published for download (e.g. on Zenodo). Everyone then gets them with:

```bash
omero-screen models pull <set-name>
```

and selects them with `[segmentation] model_set = "<set-name>"`. The Hochegger
lab's models are the `hocheggerlab` set of the `sussex` profile.
